newsitem.title: UK: Willetts denies trying to shape UK sleaze probe.
newsitem.headline: Willetts denies trying to shape UK sleaze probe.

text.p: Junior minister David Willetts denied on Monday that he tried to influence a parliamentary investigation of the "cash-for-questions" affair involving former trade minister Neil Hamilton.

In a memo to parliament's Standards and Privileges Committee, Willetts said there was nothing improper about a conversation he had when he was a whip in October 1994 with Sir Geoffrey Johnson-Smith, chairman of the now-disbanded committee on members' interests.
"I did not attempt in any manner, nor at any time, to "pressurise the committee' nor would it have been proper for me to have done so," Willetts said in his note.

The all-party committee is investigating whether Willetts breached parliament's rules by interfering with Johnson-Smith's handling of the affair, proposing to either rush it through or kick it into the long grass.
In the run-up to the general election, the incident has great potential to damage Prime Minister John Major by putting the party's reputation for sleaze and impropriety back int he spotlight.

Willetts explained that the note he made of the conversation with Johnson-Smith -- leaked to the press in October -- was so detailed because, having just joined the whips' office, he mistakenly assumed that a structured account was required.
"I regret if my note, written in my first full week of work as a whip, should have inadvertently led to any confusion or misconception as to what actually occurred," Willetts said.
Johnson-Smith strongly denied having been influenced by Willetts, who he said had "an obviously inquiring mind".
Willetts wrote at the end of his note "he wants our advice", but Johnson-Smith told the televised hearing: "I neither sought advice nor did I expect anyone to give me advice."
